7.5.49 SRFI-207 String-notated bytevectors
------------------------------------------

SRFI-207 (http://srfi.schemers.org/srfi-207/srfi-207.html) provides a
more human-friendly representation for binary-data via an ASCII text
notation for *note Bytevectors::.  It also provides bytestring-oriented
procedures for constructing bytevectors from sequences of integers,
characters, strings, and other bytevectors, and procedures for
manipulating bytevectors as if they were strings.

   Binary file formats are usually not self-describing, and if they are,
the descriptive portion is itself binary, which makes it hard for human
beings to interpret.  To assist with this problem, it is common to have
a human-readable section at the beginning of the file, or in some cases
at the beginning of each distinct section of the file.  For historical
reasons and to avoid text encoding complications, it is usual for this
human-readable section to be expressed as ASCII text.

   For example, ZIP files begin with the hex bytes â€˜50 4Bâ€™ which are the
ASCII encoding for the characters "PK", the initials of Phil Katz, the
inventor of ZIP format.  As another example, the GIF image format begins
with â€˜47 49 46 38 39 61â€™, the ASCII encoding for "GIF89a", where "89a"
is the format version.  A third example is the PNG image format, where
the file header begins â€˜89 50 4E 47â€™.  The first byte is intentionally
non-ASCII, but the next three are "PNG". Furthermore, a PNG file is
divided into chunks, each of which contains a 4-byte "chunk type" code.
The letters in the chunk type are mnemonics for its purpose, such as
"PLTE" for a palette, "bKGD" for a default background color, and "iTXt"
for descriptive text in UTF-8.

   When bytevectors contain string data of this kind, it is much more
tractable for human programmers to deal with â€˜#u8"\x89;PNG\r\n\x1A;\n"â€™
rather than â€˜#u8(0x89 0x50 0x4E 0x47 0x0D 0x0A 0x1A 0x0A)â€™.

   In addition, this SRFI provides bytevectors with additional
procedures that closely resemble those provided for strings.  For
example, bytevectors can be padded or trimmed, compared case-sensitively
or case-insensitively, searched, joined, and split.

   Most of the procedures of this SRFI begin with â€˜bytestring-â€™ in order
to distinguish them from other bytevector procedures.  This does not
mean that they accept or return a separate bytestring type: bytestrings
and bytevectors are exactly the same type.

7.5.49.1 External Notation
..........................

The basic form of a string-notated bytevector is â€˜#u8"CONTENT"â€™.  The
Scheme reader will read them if bytestrings are enabled via
â€˜(read-enable 'bytestrings)â€™, and the Scheme writer will write them if
they are enabled via â€˜(print-enable 'bytestrings)â€™.

   To avoid character encoding issues within string-notated bytevectors,
only printable ASCII characters (that is, Unicode codepoints in the
range from U+0020 to U+007E inclusive) are allowed to be used within the
CONTENT of a string-notated bytevector.  All other characters must be
expressed through mnemonic or inline hex escapes, and â€˜"â€™ and â€˜\â€™ must
also be escaped as in normal Scheme strings.

   Within the CONTENT of a string-notated bytevector:

   â€¢ â€˜\aâ€™ â‡’ 7
   â€¢ â€˜\bâ€™ â‡’ 8
   â€¢ â€˜\tâ€™ â‡’ 9
   â€¢ â€˜\nâ€™ â‡’ 10
   â€¢ â€˜\râ€™ â‡’ 13
   â€¢ â€˜\"â€™ â‡’ 34
   â€¢ â€˜\\â€™ â‡’ 92
   â€¢ â€˜\|â€™ â‡’ 124
   â€¢ the sequence â€˜\xâ€™ followed by zero or more â€˜0â€™ characters, followed
     by one or two hexadecimal digits, followed by â€˜;â€™ represents the
     integer specified by the hexadecimal digits;
   â€¢ the sequence â€˜\â€™ followed by zero or more intraline whitespace
     characters, followed by a newline, followed by zero or more further
     intraline whitespace characters, is ignored and corresponds to no
     entry in the resulting bytevector;
   â€¢ any other printable ASCII character represents the character number
     of that character in the ASCII/Unicode code chart; and
   â€¢ it is an error to use any other character or sequence beginning
     with â€˜\â€™ within a string-notated bytevector.

   Note: The â€˜\|â€™ sequence is provided so that string parsing, symbol
parsing, and string-notated bytevector parsing can all use the same
sequences.  However, we give a complete definition of the valid lexical
syntax in this SRFI rather than inheriting the native syntax of strings,
so that it is clear that â€˜#u8"&iota;"â€™ and â€˜#u8"\xE000;"â€™ are invalid.

   When the Scheme reader encounters a string-notated bytevector, it
produces a datum as if that bytevector had been written out in full.
That is, â€˜#u8"A"â€™ is exactly equivalent to â€˜#u8(65)â€™.

7.5.49.2 Constructors
.....................

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring part ...
     Converts earch PART into a sequence of small integers and returns a
     bytevector of the corresponding bytes as follows:
        â€¢ If PART is an exact integer in the range 0-255 inclusive, it
          is added to the result.
        â€¢ If PART is an ASCII character (that is, its codepoint is in
          the range 0-127 inclusive), it is converted to its codepoint
          and added to the result.
        â€¢ If PART is a bytevector, its elements are added to the result.
        â€¢ If PART is a string of ASCII characters, it is converted to a
          sequence of codepoints which are added to the result.

     Otherwise, an error satisfying â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is signaled, for
     example:

          (bytestring "lo" #\r #x65 #u8(#x6d)) â‡’ #u8"lorem"

          (bytestring "Î·" #\space #u8(#x65 #x71 #x75 #x69 #x76))
          â‡’ raised &bytestring-error

 -- Scheme Procedure: make-bytestring parts
     If the PARTS are suitable arguments for â€˜bytestringâ€™, returns the
     bytevector that would result from applying â€˜bytestringâ€™ to them.
     Otherwise, an error satisfying â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is raised.

 -- Scheme Procedure: make-bytestring! bytevector at parts
     If the PARTS are suitable arguments for â€˜bytestringâ€™, writes the
     bytes of the bytevector that would be the result of calling
     â€˜make-bytestringâ€™ into BYTEVECTOR starting at index AT.  For
     example:

          (define bv (make-bytevector 10 #x20))
          (make-bytestring! bv 2 '(#\s #\c "he" #u8(#x6d #x65))) bv)
          â‡’ #u8" scheme "

7.5.49.3 Conversion
...................

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytevector->hex-string bytevector
 -- Scheme Procedure: hex-string->bytevecto string
     Converts between a bytevector and a string containing pairs of
     hexadecimal digits.  If STRING is not pairs of hexadecimal digits,
     an error satisfying â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is raised

          (bytevector->hex-string #u8"Ford") â‡’ "467f7264"
          (hex-string->bytevector "5a6170686f64") â‡’ #u8"Zaphod")

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytevector->base64 bytevector [digits]
 -- Scheme Procedure: base64->bytevecto string [digits]
     Converts between a bytevector and its base-64 encoding as a string.
     The 64 digits are represented by the characters 0-9, A-Z, a-z, and
     the symbols + and /.  However, there are different variants of
     base-64 encoding which use different representations of the 62nd
     and 63rd digit.  If the optional argument DIGITS (a two-character
     string) is provided, those two characters will be used as the 62nd
     and 63rd digit instead.  Details can be found in RFC 4648
     (https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4648).

     If STRING is not in base-64 format, an error satisfying
     â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is raised.  However, characters that satisfy
     â€˜char-whitespace?â€™ are silently ignored.

          (bytevector->base64 #u8(1 2 3 4 5 6)) â‡’ â‡’ "AQIDBAUG"
          (bytevector->base64 #u8"Arthur Dent") â‡’ "QXJ0aHVyIERlbnQ="
          (base64->bytevector "+/     /+") â‡’ #u8(#xfb #xff #xfe)

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring->list bytevector [start [end]]
     Converts all or part of a bytevector into a list of the same length
     containing characters for elements in the range 32 to 127 and exact
     integers for all other elements.</p>

          (bytestring->list #u8(#x41 #x42 1 2) 1 3) â‡’ (#\B 1)

 -- Scheme Procedure: make-bytestring-generator arg ...
     Returns a generator that when invoked will return consecutive bytes
     of the bytevector that â€˜bytestringâ€™ would create when applied to
     ARGS, but without creating any bytevectors.  The ARGS are validated
     before any bytes are generated; if they are ill-formed, an error
     satisfying â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is raised.

          (generator->list (make-bytestring-generator "lorem"))
          â‡’ (#x6c #x6f #x72 #x65 #x6d)

7.5.49.4 Selection
..................

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-pad bytevector len char-or-u8
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-pad-right bytevector len char-or-u8
     Returns a newly allocated bytevector with the contents of
     BYTEVECTOR plus sufficient additional bytes at the beginning/end
     containing CHAR-OR-U8 (which can be either an ASCII character or an
     exact integer in the range 0-255) such that the length of the
     result is at least LEN.

          (bytestring-pad #u8"Zaphod" 10 #\_) â‡’ #u8"____Zaphod"
          (bytestring-pad-right #u8(#x80 #x7f) 8 0) â‡’ #u8(#x80 #x7f 0 0 0 0 0 0)

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-trim bytevector pred
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-trim-right bytevector pred
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-trim-both bytevector pred
     Returns a newly allocated bytevector with the contents of
     BYTEVECTOR, except that consecutive bytes at the beginning / the
     end / both the beginning and the end that satisfy PRED are not
     included.

          (bytestring-trim #u8"   Trillian" (lambda (b) (= b #x20)))
          â‡’ #u8"Trillian"
          (bytestring-trim-both #u8(0 0 #x80 #x7f 0 0 0) zero?) â‡’ #u8(#x80 #x7f)

7.5.49.5 Replacement
....................

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-replace bytevector1 bytevector2 start1
          end1 [start2 end2]
     Returns a newly allocated bytevector with the contents of
     BYTEVECTOR1, except that the bytes indexed by START1 and END1 are
     not included but are replaced by the bytes of BYTEVECTOR2 indexed
     by START2 and END2.

          (bytestring-replace #u8"Vogon torture" #u8"poetry" 6 13)
          â‡’ #u8"Vogon poetry"

7.5.49.6 Comparison
...................

To compare bytevectors for equality, use the â€˜bytevector=?â€™ procedure
from â€˜(rnrs bytevectors)â€™ (*note Bytevectors::) or â€˜equal?â€™.

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring<? bytevector1 bytevector2
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring>? bytevector1 bytevector2
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring<=? bytevector1 bytevector2
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring>=? bytevector1 bytevector2
     Returns â€˜#tâ€™ if BYTEVECTOR1 is less than / greater than / less than
     or equal to / greater than or equal to BYTEVECTOR2.  Comparisons
     are lexicographical: shorter bytevectors compare before longer
     ones, all elements being equal.

          (bytestring<? #u8"Heart Of Gold" #u8"Heart of Gold") â‡’ #t
          (bytestring<=? #u8(#x81 #x95) #u8(#x80 #xa0)) â‡’ #f
          (bytestring>? #u8(1 2 3) #u8(1 2)) â‡’ #t

7.5.49.7 Searching
..................

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-index bytevector pred [start [end]]
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-index-right bytevector pred [start
          [end]]
     Searches BYTEVECTOR from START to END / from END to START for the
     first byte that satisfies PRED, and returns the index into
     BYTEVECTOR containing that byte.  In either direction, START is
     inclusive and END is exclusive.  If there are no such bytes,
     returns â€˜#fâ€™.

          (bytestring-index #u8(#x65 #x72 #x83 #x6f) (Î» (b) (> b #x7f))) â‡’ 2
          (bytestring-index #u8"Beeblebrox" (Î» (b) (> b #x7f))) â‡’ #f
          (bytestring-index-right #u8"Zaphod" odd?) â‡’ 4

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-break bytevector pred
 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-span bytevector pred
     Returns two values, a bytevector containing the maximal sequence of
     characters (searching from the beginning of BYTEVECTOR to the end)
     that do not satisfy / do satisfy PRED, and another bytevector
     containing the remaining characters.

          (bytestring-break #u8(#x50 #x4b 0 0 #x1 #x5) zero?)
            â‡’ #u8(#x50 #x4b) #u8(0 0 #x1 #x5)
          (bytestring-span #u8"ABCDefg" (lambda (b) (and (> b 40) (< b 91))))
            â‡’ #u8"ABCD" #u8"efg"

7.5.49.8 Joining And Splitting
..............................

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-join bytevector-list delimiter
     Joins the bytevectors in BYTEVECTOR-LIST together using the
     DELIMITER, which can be anything suitable as an argument to
     â€˜bytestringâ€™.  The GRAMMAR argument is a symbol that determines how
     the delimiter is used, and defaults to â€˜infixâ€™.  It is an error for
     grammar to be any symbol other than these four:

     â€˜infixâ€™
          means an infix or separator grammar: inserts the delimiter
          between list elements.  An empty list will produce an empty
          bytevector
     â€˜strict-infixâ€™
          means the same as â€˜infixâ€™ if the list is non-empty, but will
          signal an error satisfying â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ if given an
          empty list.
     â€˜suffixâ€™
          means a suffix or terminator grammar: inserts the delimiter
          after every list element.
     â€˜prefixâ€™
          means a prefix grammar: inserts the delimiter before every
          list element.

     For example:
          (bytestring-join '(#u8"Heart" #u8"of" #u8"Gold") #x20)
            â‡’ #u8"Heart of Gold"
          (bytestring-join '(#u8(#xef #xbb) #u8(#xbf)) 0 'prefix)
            â‡’ #u8(0 #xef #xbb 0 #xbf)
          (bytestring-join '() 0 'strict-infix)
            â‡’ â‡’ raised &bytestring-error

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytestring-split bytevector delimiter [grammar]
     Divides the elements of BYTEVECTOR and returns a list of newly
     allocated bytevectors using the DELIMITER (an ASCII character or
     exact integer in the range 0-255 inclusive).  Delimiter bytes are
     not included in the result bytevectors.

     The GRAMMAR argument is used to control how BYTEVECTOR is divided.
     It has the same default and meaning as in â€˜bytestring-joinâ€™, except
     that â€˜infixâ€™ and â€˜strict-infixâ€™ mean the same thing.  That is, if
     GRAMMAR is â€˜prefixâ€™ or â€˜suffixâ€™, then ignore any delimiter in the
     first or last position of BYTEVECTOR respectively.

          (bytestring-split #u8"Beeblebrox" #x62)
            â‡’ (#u8"Bee" #u8"le" #u8"rox")
          (bytestring-split #u8(1 0 2 0) 0 'suffix)
            â‡’ (#u8(1) #u8(2))

7.5.49.9 I/O
............

 -- Scheme Procedure: read-textual-bytestring prefix [port]
     Reads a string in the external format described in this SRFI from
     PORT and return it as a bytevector.  If the PREFIX argument is
     false, this procedure assumes that "â€˜#u8â€™" has already been read
     from PORT.  If PORT is omitted, it defaults to the value of
     â€˜(current-input-port)â€™.  If the characters read are not in the
     external format, an error satisfying â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is raised.

          (call-with-port
              (open-input-string "#u8\"AB\\xad;\\xf0;\\x0d;CD\"")
            (lambda (port) (read-textual-bytestring #t port)))
          â‡’ #u8(#x41 #x42 #xad #xf0 #x0d #x43 #x44)

 -- Scheme Procedure: write-textual-bytestring bytevector [port]
     Writes BYTEVECTOR in the external format described in this SRFI to
     PORT.  Bytes representing non-graphical ASCII characters are
     unencoded: all other bytes are encoded with a single letter if
     possible, otherwise with a â€˜\xâ€™ escape.  If PORT is omitted, it
     defaults to the value of â€˜(current-output-port)â€™.

          (call-with-port
              (open-output-string)
            (lambda (port)
              (write-textual-bytestring
               #u8(#x9 #x41 #x72 #x74 #x68 #x75 #x72 #xa)
               port)
              (get-output-string port)))
          â‡’ "#u8\"\\tArthur\\n\""

 -- Scheme Procedure: write-binary-bytestring port arg ...
     Outputs each ARG to the binary output port PORT using the same
     interpretations as â€˜bytestringâ€™, but without creating any
     bytevectors.  The ARGS are validated before any bytes are written
     to PORT; if they are ill-formed, an error satisfying
     â€˜bytestring-error?â€™ is raised.

          (call-with-port
              (open-output-bytevector)
            (lambda (port)
              (write-binary-bytestring port #\Z #x61 #x70 "hod")
              (get-output-bytevector port)))
          â‡’ #u8"Zaphod"

7.5.49.11 Acknowledgements
..........................

Daphne Preston-Kendal devised the string notation for bytevectors; John
Cowan, the procedure library; Wolfgang Corcoran-Mathe, the original,
sample implementation of the procedures.

   The notation is inspired by the notation used in Python since version
2.6 for â€˜bytesâ€™ objects, which are fundamentally similar in purpose to
Scheme bytevectors, especially in R7RS. In addition, many of the
procedures are closely analogous to those of SRFI 152
(https://srfi.schemers.org/srfi-152/srfi-152.html).

   Thanks is also due to the participants in the SRFI mailing list.  In
particular: Lassi Kortela corrected an embarrassing technical error;
Marc Nieper-WiÃŸkirchen explained why the â€˜writeâ€™ procedure ought not to
be allowed to use this notation by default.

7.5.50 SRFI-244 - Multiple-value Definitions
--------------------------------------------

The implementation of this SRFI re-exports the â€˜define-valuesâ€™ form
described in *note Binding Multiple Values::.

7.6 R6RS Support
================

*Note R6RS Libraries::, for more information on how to define R6RS
libraries, and their integration with Guile modules.

7.6.1 Incompatibilities with the R6RS
-------------------------------------

There are some incompatibilities between Guile and the R6RS. Some of
them are intentional, some of them are bugs, and some are simply
unimplemented features.  Please let the Guile developers know if you
find one that is not on this list.

   â€¢ The R6RS specifies many situations in which a conforming
     implementation must signal a specific error.  Guile doesnâ€™t really
     care about that too muchâ€”if a correct R6RS program would not hit
     that error, we donâ€™t bother checking for it.

   â€¢ Multiple â€˜libraryâ€™ forms in one file are not yet supported.  This
     is because the expansion of â€˜libraryâ€™ sets the current module, but
     does not restore it.  This is a bug.

   â€¢ R6RS unicode escapes within strings are disabled by default,
     because they conflict with Guileâ€™s already-existing escapes.  The
     same is the case for R6RS treatment of escaped newlines in strings.

     R6RS behavior can be turned on via a reader option.  *Note String
     Syntax::, for more information.

   â€¢ Guile does not yet support Unicode escapes in symbols, such as
     â€˜H\x65;lloâ€™ (the same as â€˜Helloâ€™), or â€˜\x3BB;â€™ (the same as â€˜Î»â€™).

   â€¢ A â€˜set!â€™ to a variable transformer may only expand to an
     expression, not a definitionâ€”even if the original â€˜set!â€™ expression
     was in definition context.

   â€¢ Instead of using the algorithm detailed in chapter 10 of the R6RS,
     expansion of toplevel forms happens sequentially.

     For example, while the expansion of the following set of toplevel
     definitions does the correct thing:

          (begin
           (define even?
             (lambda (x)
               (or (= x 0) (odd? (- x 1)))))
           (define-syntax odd?
             (syntax-rules ()
               ((odd? x) (not (even? x)))))
           (even? 10))
          â‡’ #t

     The same definitions outside of the â€˜beginâ€™ wrapper do not:

          (define even?
            (lambda (x)
              (or (= x 0) (odd? (- x 1)))))
          (define-syntax odd?
            (syntax-rules ()
              ((odd? x) (not (even? x)))))
          (even? 10)
          <unnamed port>:4:18: In procedure even?:
          <unnamed port>:4:18: Wrong type to apply: #<syntax-transformer odd?>

     This is because when expanding the right-hand-side of â€˜even?â€™, the
     reference to â€˜odd?â€™ is not yet marked as a syntax transformer, so
     it is assumed to be a function.

     This bug will only affect top-level programs, not code in â€˜libraryâ€™
     forms.  Fixing it for toplevel forms seems doable, but tricky to
     implement in a backward-compatible way.  Suggestions and/or patches
     would be appreciated.

   â€¢ The â€˜(rnrs io ports)â€™ module is incomplete.  Work is ongoing to fix
     this.

   â€¢ Guile does not prevent use of textual I/O procedures on binary
     ports, or vice versa.  All ports in Guile support both binary and
     textual I/O. *Note Encoding::, for full details.

   â€¢ Guileâ€™s implementation of â€˜equal?â€™ may fail to terminate when
     applied to arguments containing cycles.

   Guile exposes a procedure in the root module to choose R6RS defaults
over Guileâ€™s historical defaults.

 -- Scheme Procedure: install-r6rs!
     Alter Guileâ€™s default settings to better conform to the R6RS.

     While Guileâ€™s defaults may evolve over time, the current changes
     that this procedure imposes are to add â€˜.slsâ€™ and â€˜.guile.slsâ€™ to
     the set of supported â€˜%load-extensionsâ€™, to better support R6RS
     conventions.  *Note Load Paths::.  Also, enable R6RS unicode
     escapes in strings; see the discussion above.

   Finally, note that the â€˜--r6rsâ€™ command-line argument will call
â€˜install-r6rs!â€™ before calling user code.  R6RS users probably want to
pass this argument to their Guile.

7.6.2 R6RS Standard Libraries
-----------------------------

In contrast with earlier versions of the Revised Report, the R6RS
organizes the procedures and syntactic forms required of conforming
implementations into a set of â€œstandard librariesâ€ which can be imported
as necessary by user programs and libraries.  Here we briefly list the
libraries that have been implemented for Guile.

   We do not attempt to document these libraries fully here, as most of
their functionality is already available in Guile itself.  The
expectation is that most Guile users will use the well-known and
well-documented Guile modules.  These R6RS libraries are mostly useful
to users who want to port their code to other R6RS systems.

   The documentation in the following sections reproduces some of the
content of the library section of the Report, but is mostly intended to
provide supplementary information about Guileâ€™s implementation of the
R6RS standard libraries.  For complete documentation, design rationales
and further examples, we advise you to consult the â€œStandard Librariesâ€
section of the Report (*note R6RS Standard Libraries: (r6rs)Standard
Libraries.).

7.6.2.1 Library Usage
.....................

Guile implements the R6RS â€˜libraryâ€™ form as a transformation to a native
Guile module definition.  As a consequence of this, all of the libraries
described in the following subsections, in addition to being available
for use by R6RS libraries and top-level programs, can also be imported
as if they were normal Guile modulesâ€”via a â€˜use-modulesâ€™ form, say.  For
example, the R6RS â€œcompositeâ€ library can be imported by:

       (import (rnrs (6)))

       (use-modules ((rnrs) :version (6)))

   For more information on Guileâ€™s library implementation, see (*note
R6RS Libraries::).

 -- Scheme Procedure: div-and-mod x y
     These procedures accept two real numbers X and Y, where the divisor
     Y must be non-zero.  â€˜divâ€™ returns the integer Q and â€˜modâ€™ returns
     the real number R such that X = Q*Y + R and 0 <= R < abs(Y).
     â€˜div-and-modâ€™ returns both Q and R, and is more efficient than
     computing each separately.  Note that when Y > 0, â€˜divâ€™ returns
     floor(X/Y), otherwise it returns ceiling(X/Y).

          (div 123 10) â‡’ 12
          (mod 123 10) â‡’ 3
          (div-and-mod 123 10) â‡’ 12 and 3
          (div-and-mod 123 -10) â‡’ -12 and 3
          (div-and-mod -123 10) â‡’ -13 and 7
          (div-and-mod -123 -10) â‡’ 13 and 7
          (div-and-mod -123.2 -63.5) â‡’ 2.0 and 3.8
          (div-and-mod 16/3 -10/7) â‡’ -3 and 22/21

 -- Scheme Procedure: div0 x y
 -- Scheme Procedure: mod0 x y
 -- Scheme Procedure: div0-and-mod0 x y
     These procedures accept two real numbers X and Y, where the divisor
     Y must be non-zero.  â€˜div0â€™ returns the integer Q and â€˜mod0â€™
     returns the real number R such that X = Q*Y + R and -abs(Y/2) <= R
     < abs(Y/2).  â€˜div0-and-mod0â€™ returns both Q and R, and is more
     efficient than computing each separately.

     Note that â€˜div0â€™ returns X/Y rounded to the nearest integer.  When
     X/Y lies exactly half-way between two integers, the tie is broken
     according to the sign of Y.  If Y > 0, ties are rounded toward
     positive infinity, otherwise they are rounded toward negative
     infinity.  This is a consequence of the requirement that -abs(Y/2)
     <= R < abs(Y/2).

          (div0 123 10) â‡’ 12
          (mod0 123 10) â‡’ 3
          (div0-and-mod0 123 10) â‡’ 12 and 3
          (div0-and-mod0 123 -10) â‡’ -12 and 3
          (div0-and-mod0 -123 10) â‡’ -12 and -3
          (div0-and-mod0 -123 -10) â‡’ 12 and -3
          (div0-and-mod0 -123.2 -63.5) â‡’ 2.0 and 3.8
          (div0-and-mod0 16/3 -10/7) â‡’ -4 and -8/21

 -- Scheme Procedure: real-valued? obj
 -- Scheme Procedure: rational-valued? obj
 -- Scheme Procedure: integer-valued? obj
     These procedures return â€˜#tâ€™ if and only if their arguments can,
     respectively, be coerced to a real, rational, or integer value
     without a loss of numerical precision.

     â€˜real-valued?â€™ will return â€˜#tâ€™ for complex numbers whose imaginary
     parts are zero.

 -- Scheme Procedure: nan? x
 -- Scheme Procedure: infinite? x
 -- Scheme Procedure: finite? x
     â€˜nan?â€™ returns â€˜#tâ€™ if X is a NaN value, â€˜#fâ€™ otherwise.
     â€˜infinite?â€™ returns â€˜#tâ€™ if X is an infinite value, â€˜#fâ€™ otherwise.
     â€˜finite?â€™ returns â€˜#tâ€™ if X is neither infinite nor a NaN value,
     otherwise it returns â€˜#fâ€™.  Every real number satisfies exactly one
     of these predicates.  An exception is raised if X is not real.

 -- Scheme Syntax: assert expr
     Raises an â€˜&assertionâ€™ condition if EXPR evaluates to â€˜#fâ€™;
     otherwise evaluates to the value of EXPR.

 -- Scheme Procedure: error who message irritant1 ...
 -- Scheme Procedure: assertion-violation who message irritant1 ...
     These procedures raise compound conditions based on their
     arguments: If WHO is not â€˜#fâ€™, the condition will include a â€˜&whoâ€™
     condition whose â€˜whoâ€™ field is set to WHO; a â€˜&messageâ€™ condition
     will be included with a â€˜messageâ€™ field equal to MESSAGE; an
     â€˜&irritantsâ€™ condition will be included with its â€˜irritantsâ€™ list
     given by â€˜irritant1 ...â€™.

     â€˜errorâ€™ produces a compound condition with the simple conditions
     described above, as well as an â€˜&errorâ€™ condition;
     â€˜assertion-violationâ€™ produces one that includes an â€˜&assertionâ€™

7.6.2.8 R6RS Records
....................

The manual sections below describe Guileâ€™s implementation of R6RS
records, which provide support for user-defined data types.  The R6RS
records API provides a superset of the features provided by Guileâ€™s
â€œnativeâ€ records, as well as those of the SRFI-9 records API; *Note
Records::, and *note SRFI-9 Records::, for a description of those
interfaces.

   As with SRFI-9 and Guileâ€™s native records, R6RS records are
constructed using a record-type descriptor that specifies attributes
like the recordâ€™s name, its fields, and the mutability of those fields.

   R6RS records extend this framework to support single inheritance via
the specification of a â€œparentâ€ type for a record type at definition
time.  Accessors and mutator procedures for the fields of a parent type
may be applied to records of a subtype of this parent.  A record type
may be â€œsealedâ€, in which case it cannot be used as the parent of
another record type.

   The inheritance mechanism for record types also informs the process
of initializing the fields of a record and its parents.  Constructor
procedures that generate new instances of a record type are obtained
from a record constructor descriptor, which encapsulates the record-type
descriptor of the record to be constructed along with a â€œprotocolâ€
procedure that defines how constructors for record subtypes delegate to
the constructors of their parent types.

   A protocol is a procedure used by the record system at construction
time to bind arguments to the fields of the record being constructed.
The protocol procedure is passed a procedure N that accepts the
arguments required to construct the recordâ€™s parent type; this
procedure, when invoked, will return a procedure P that accepts the
arguments required to construct a new instance of the record type itself
and returns a new instance of the record type.

   The protocol should in turn return a procedure that uses N and P to
initialize the fields of the record type and its parent type(s).  This
procedure will be the constructor returned by

   As a trivial example, consider the hypothetical record type â€˜pixelâ€™,
which encapsulates an x-y location on a screen, and â€˜voxelâ€™, which has
â€˜pixelâ€™ as its parent type and stores an additional coordinate.  The
following protocol produces a constructor procedure that accepts all
three coordinates, uses the first two to initialize the fields of
â€˜pixelâ€™, and binds the third to the single field of â€˜voxelâ€™.

       (lambda (n)
         (lambda (x y z)
           (let ((p (n x y)))
             (p z))))

   It may be helpful to think of protocols as â€œconstructor factoriesâ€
that produce chains of delegating constructors glued together by the
helper procedure N.

   An R6RS record type may be declared to be â€œnongenerativeâ€ via the use
of a unique generated or user-supplied symbolâ€”or â€œuidâ€â€”such that
subsequent record type declarations with the same uid and attributes
will return the previously-declared record-type descriptor.

   R6RS record types may also be declared to be â€œopaqueâ€, in which case
the various predicates and introspection procedures defined in â€˜(rnrs
records introspection)â€™ will behave as if records of this type are not
records at all.

   Note that while the R6RS records API shares much of its namespace
with both the SRFI-9 and native Guile records APIs, it is not currently
compatible with either.

7.6.2.9 rnrs records syntactic
..............................

The â€˜(rnrs records syntactic (6))â€™ library exports the syntactic API for
working with R6RS records.

 -- Scheme Syntax: define-record-type name-spec record-clause ...
     Defines a new record type, introducing bindings for a record-type
     descriptor, a record constructor descriptor, a constructor
     procedure, a record predicate, and accessor and mutator procedures
     for the new record typeâ€™s fields.

     NAME-SPEC must either be an identifier or must take the form
     â€˜(record-name constructor-name predicate-name)â€™, where RECORD-NAME,
     CONSTRUCTOR-NAME, and PREDICATE-NAME are all identifiers and
     specify the names to which, respectively, the record-type
     descriptor, constructor, and predicate procedures will be bound.
     If NAME-SPEC is only an identifier, it specifies the name to which
     the generated record-type descriptor will be bound.

     Each RECORD-CLAUSE must be one of the following:

        â€¢ â€˜(fields field-spec*)â€™, where each FIELD-SPEC specifies a
          field of the new record type and takes one of the following
          forms:
             â€¢ â€˜(immutable field-name accessor-name)â€™, which specifies
               an immutable field with the name FIELD-NAME and binds an
               accessor procedure for it to the name given by
               ACCESSOR-NAME
             â€¢ â€˜(mutable field-name accessor-name mutator-name)â€™, which
               specifies a mutable field with the name FIELD-NAME and
               binds accessor and mutator procedures to ACCESSOR-NAME
               and MUTATOR-NAME, respectively
             â€¢ â€˜(immutable field-name)â€™, which specifies an immutable
               field with the name FIELD-NAME; an accessor procedure for
               it will be created and named by appending record name and
               FIELD-NAME with a hyphen separator
             â€¢ â€˜(mutable field-nameâ€™), which specifies a mutable field
               with the name FIELD-NAME; an accessor procedure for it
               will be created and named as described above; a mutator
               procedure will also be created and named by appending
               â€˜-set!â€™ to the accessor name
             â€¢ â€˜field-nameâ€™, which specifies an immutable field with the
               name FIELD-NAME; an access procedure for it will be
               created and named as described above
        â€¢ â€˜(parent parent-name)â€™, where PARENT-NAME is a symbol giving
          the name of the record type to be used as the parent of the
          new record type
        â€¢ â€˜(protocol expression)â€™, where EXPRESSION evaluates to a
          protocol procedure which behaves as described above, and is
          used to create a record constructor descriptor for the new
          record type
        â€¢ â€˜(sealed sealed?)â€™, where SEALED? is a boolean value that
          specifies whether or not the new record type is sealed
        â€¢ â€˜(opaque opaque?)â€™, where OPAQUE? is a boolean value that
          specifies whether or not the new record type is opaque
        â€¢ â€˜(nongenerative [uid])â€™, which specifies that the record type
          is nongenerative via the optional uid UID.  If UID is not
          specified, a unique uid will be generated at expansion time
        â€¢ â€˜(parent-rtd parent-rtd parent-cd)â€™, a more explicit form of
          the â€˜parentâ€™ form above; PARENT-RTD and PARENT-CD should
          evaluate to a record-type descriptor and a record constructor
          descriptor, respectively

 -- Scheme Syntax: record-type-descriptor record-name
     Evaluates to the record-type descriptor associated with the type
     specified by RECORD-NAME.

 -- Scheme Syntax: record-constructor-descriptor record-name
     Evaluates to the record-constructor descriptor associated with the
     type specified by RECORD-NAME.

7.6.2.10 rnrs records procedural
................................

The â€˜(rnrs records procedural (6))â€™ library exports the procedural API
for working with R6RS records.

 -- Scheme Procedure: make-record-type-descriptor name parent uid
          sealed? opaque? fields
     Returns a new record-type descriptor with the specified
     characteristics: NAME must be a symbol giving the name of the new
     record type; PARENT must be either â€˜#fâ€™ or a non-sealed record-type
     descriptor for the returned record type to extend; UID must be
     either â€˜#fâ€™, indicating that the record type is generative, or a
     symbol giving the typeâ€™s nongenerative uid; SEALED? and OPAQUE?
     must be boolean values that specify the sealedness and opaqueness
     of the record type; FIELDS must be a vector of zero or more field
     specifiers of the form â€˜(mutable name)â€™ or â€˜(immutable name)â€™,
     where name is a symbol giving a name for the field.

     If UID is not â€˜#fâ€™, it must be a symbol

 -- Scheme Procedure: record-type-descriptor? obj
     Returns â€˜#tâ€™ if OBJ is a record-type descriptor, â€˜#fâ€™ otherwise.

 -- Scheme Procedure: make-record-constructor-descriptor rtd
          parent-constructor-descriptor protocol
     Returns a new record constructor descriptor that can be used to
     produce constructors for the record type specified by the
     record-type descriptor RTD and whose delegation and binding
     behavior are specified by the protocol procedure PROTOCOL.

     PARENT-CONSTRUCTOR-DESCRIPTOR specifies a record constructor

     also be â€˜#fâ€™ in this case.

 -- Scheme Procedure: record-constructor rcd
     Returns a record constructor procedure by invoking the protocol
     defined by the record-constructor descriptor RCD.

 -- Scheme Procedure: record-predicate rtd
     Returns the record predicate procedure for the record-type
     descriptor RTD.

 -- Scheme Procedure: record-accessor rtd k
     Returns the record field accessor procedure for the Kth field of
     the record-type descriptor RTD.

 -- Scheme Procedure: record-mutator rtd k
     Returns the record field mutator procedure for the Kth field of the
     record-type descriptor RTD.  An â€˜&assertionâ€™ condition will be
     raised if this field is not mutable.

7.6.2.12 rnrs exceptions

The â€˜(rnrs exceptions (6))â€™ library provides functionality related to

pre-R6RS facility.  In Guile, SRFI-34, SRFI-35, and R6RS exception
handling are all built on the same core facilities, and so are

 -- Scheme Procedure: with-exception-handler handler thunk

     â€˜with-exception-handlerâ€™.

 -- Scheme Syntax: guard (variable clause1 clause2 ...) body
     Evaluates the expression given by BODY, first creating an ad hoc

     then evaluates the specified CLAUSEs as if they were part of a
     â€˜condâ€™ expression, with the value of the first matching clause
     becoming the value of the â€˜guardâ€™ expression (*note
     Conditionals::).  If none of the clauseâ€™s test expressions
     evaluates to â€˜#tâ€™, the exception is re-raised, with the exception
     handler that was current before the evaluation of the â€˜guardâ€™ form.

     For example, the expression

          (guard (ex ((eq? ex 'foo) 'bar) ((eq? ex 'bar) 'baz))
            (raise 'bar))

 -- Scheme Procedure: raise obj
     Equivalent to core Guile â€˜(raise-exception OBJ)â€™.  *Note Raising

 -- Scheme Procedure: raise-continuable obj

     *Note Raising and Handling Exceptions::.

7.6.2.13 rnrs conditions
........................

The â€˜(rnrs condition (6))â€™ library provides forms and procedures for
constructing new condition types, as well as a library of pre-defined
condition types that represent a variety of common exceptional
situations.  Conditions are records of a subtype of the â€˜&conditionâ€™
record type, which is neither sealed nor opaque.  *Note R6RS Records::.

   Conditions may be manipulated singly, as â€œsimple conditionsâ€, or when
composed with other conditions to form â€œcompound conditionsâ€.  Compound
conditions do not â€œnestâ€â€”constructing a new compound condition out of
existing compound conditions will â€œflattenâ€ them into their component
simple conditions.  For example, making a new condition out of a
â€˜&messageâ€™ condition and a compound condition that contains an
â€˜&assertionâ€™ condition and another â€˜&messageâ€™ condition will produce a
compound condition that contains two â€˜&messageâ€™ conditions and one
â€˜&assertionâ€™ condition.

   The record type predicates and field accessors described below can
operate on either simple or compound conditions.  In the latter case,
the predicate returns â€˜#tâ€™ if the compound condition contains a
component simple condition of the appropriate type; the field accessors
return the requisite fields from the first component simple condition
found to be of the appropriate type.

   Guileâ€™s R6RS layer uses core exception types from the â€˜(ice-9
exceptions)â€™ module as the basis for its R6RS condition system.  Guile
prefers to use the term â€œexception objectâ€ and â€œexception typeâ€ rather
than â€œconditionâ€ or â€œcondition typeâ€, but thatâ€™s just a naming
difference.  Guile also has different names for the types in the
condition hierarchy.  *Note Exception Objects::, for full details.

   This library is quite similar to the SRFI-35 conditions module (*note
SRFI-35::).  Among other minor differences, the â€˜(rnrs conditions)â€™
library features slightly different semantics around condition field
accessors, and comes with a larger number of pre-defined condition
types.  The two APIs are compatible; the â€˜condition?â€™ predicate from one
API will return â€˜#tâ€™ when applied to a condition object created in the
other.  of the condition types are the same, also.

     Guile.

 -- Scheme Procedure: simple-conditions condition

     its condition arguments, flattening any specified compound
     conditions into their component simple conditions as described

     â€˜simple-conditionsâ€™ returns a list of the component simple

7.6.2.15 Transcoders
....................

The transcoder facilities are exported by â€˜(rnrs io ports)â€™.

   Several different Unicode encoding schemes describe standard ways to
encode characters and strings as byte sequences and to decode those
sequences.  Within this document, a â€œcodecâ€ is an immutable Scheme
object that represents a Unicode or similar encoding scheme.

   An â€œend-of-line styleâ€ is a symbol that, if it is not â€˜noneâ€™,
describes how a textual port transcodes representations of line endings.

   A â€œtranscoderâ€ is an immutable Scheme object that combines a codec
with an end-of-line style and a method for handling decoding errors.
Each transcoder represents some specific bidirectional (but not
necessarily lossless), possibly stateful translation between byte
sequences and Unicode characters and strings.  Every transcoder can
operate in the input direction (bytes to characters) or in the output
direction (characters to bytes).  A TRANSCODER parameter name means that
the corresponding argument must be a transcoder.

   A â€œbinary portâ€ is a port that supports binary I/O, does not have an
associated transcoder and does not support textual I/O. A â€œtextual portâ€
is a port that supports textual I/O, and does not support binary I/O. A
textual port may or may not have an associated transcoder.

 -- Scheme Procedure: latin-1-codec
 -- Scheme Procedure: utf-8-codec
 -- Scheme Procedure: utf-16-codec

     These are predefined codecs for the ISO 8859-1, UTF-8, and UTF-16
     encoding schemes.

     A call to any of these procedures returns a value that is equal in
     the sense of â€˜eqv?â€™ to the result of any other call to the same
     procedure.

 -- Scheme Syntax: eol-style EOL-STYLE-SYMBOL

     EOL-STYLE-SYMBOL should be a symbol whose name is one of â€˜lfâ€™,
     â€˜crâ€™, â€˜crlfâ€™, â€˜nelâ€™, â€˜crnelâ€™, â€˜lsâ€™, and â€˜noneâ€™.

     The form evaluates to the corresponding symbol.  If the name of
     EOL-STYLE-SYMBOL is not one of these symbols, the effect and result
     are implementation-dependent; in particular, the result may be an
     eol-style symbol acceptable as an EOL-STYLE argument to
     â€˜make-transcoderâ€™.  Otherwise, an exception is raised.

     All eol-style symbols except â€˜noneâ€™ describe a specific line-ending
     encoding:

     â€˜lfâ€™
          linefeed
     â€˜crâ€™
          carriage return
     â€˜crlfâ€™
          carriage return, linefeed
     â€˜nelâ€™
          next line
     â€˜crnelâ€™
          carriage return, next line
     â€˜lsâ€™
          line separator

     For a textual port with a transcoder, and whose transcoder has an
     eol-style symbol â€˜noneâ€™, no conversion occurs.  For a textual input
     port, any eol-style symbol other than â€˜noneâ€™ means that all of the
     above line-ending encodings are recognized and are translated into
     a single linefeed.  For a textual output port, â€˜noneâ€™ and â€˜lfâ€™ are
     equivalent.  Linefeed characters are encoded according to the
     specified eol-style symbol, and all other characters that
     participate in possible line endings are encoded as is.

          Note: Only the name of EOL-STYLE-SYMBOL is significant.

 -- Scheme Procedure: native-eol-style
     Returns the default end-of-line style of the underlying platform,
     e.g., â€˜lfâ€™ on Unix and â€˜crlfâ€™ on Windows.

 -- Condition Type: &i/o-decoding
 -- Scheme Procedure: make-i/o-decoding-error port
 -- Scheme Procedure: i/o-decoding-error? obj
     This condition type could be defined by

          (define-condition-type &i/o-decoding &i/o-port
            make-i/o-decoding-error i/o-decoding-error?)

     An exception with this type is raised when one of the operations
     for textual input from a port encounters a sequence of bytes that
     cannot be translated into a character or string by the input
     direction of the portâ€™s transcoder.

     When such an exception is raised, the portâ€™s position is past the
     invalid encoding.

 -- Condition Type: &i/o-encoding
 -- Scheme Procedure: make-i/o-encoding-error port char
 -- Scheme Procedure: i/o-encoding-error? obj
 -- Scheme Procedure: i/o-encoding-error-char condition
     This condition type could be defined by

          (define-condition-type &i/o-encoding &i/o-port
            make-i/o-encoding-error i/o-encoding-error?
            (char i/o-encoding-error-char))

     An exception with this type is raised when one of the operations
     for textual output to a port encounters a character that cannot be
     translated into bytes by the output direction of the portâ€™s
     transcoder.  CHAR is the character that could not be encoded.

 -- Scheme Syntax: error-handling-mode ERROR-HANDLING-MODE-SYMBOL
     ERROR-HANDLING-MODE-SYMBOL should be a symbol whose name is one of
     â€˜ignoreâ€™, â€˜raiseâ€™, and â€˜replaceâ€™.  The form evaluates to the
     corresponding symbol.  If ERROR-HANDLING-MODE-SYMBOL is not one of
     these identifiers, effect and result are implementation-dependent:
     The result may be an error-handling-mode symbol acceptable as a
     HANDLING-MODE argument to â€˜make-transcoderâ€™.  If it is not
     acceptable as a HANDLING-MODE argument to â€˜make-transcoderâ€™, an
     exception is raised.

          Note: Only the name of ERROR-HANDLING-MODE-SYMBOL is
          significant.

     The error-handling mode of a transcoder specifies the behavior of
     textual I/O operations in the presence of encoding or decoding
     errors.

     If a textual input operation encounters an invalid or incomplete
     character encoding, and the error-handling mode is â€˜ignoreâ€™, an
     appropriate number of bytes of the invalid encoding are ignored and
     decoding continues with the following bytes.

     If the error-handling mode is â€˜replaceâ€™, the replacement character
     U+FFFD is injected into the data stream, an appropriate number of
     bytes are ignored, and decoding continues with the following bytes.

     If the error-handling mode is â€˜raiseâ€™, an exception with condition
     type â€˜&i/o-decodingâ€™ is raised.

     If a textual output operation encounters a character it cannot
     encode, and the error-handling mode is â€˜ignoreâ€™, the character is
     ignored and encoding continues with the next character.  If the
     error-handling mode is â€˜replaceâ€™, a codec-specific replacement
     character is emitted by the transcoder, and encoding continues with
     the next character.  The replacement character is U+FFFD for
     transcoders whose codec is one of the Unicode encodings, but is the
     â€˜?â€™ character for the Latin-1 encoding.  If the error-handling mode
     is â€˜raiseâ€™, an exception with condition type â€˜&i/o-encodingâ€™ is
     raised.

 -- Scheme Procedure: make-transcoder codec
 -- Scheme Procedure: make-transcoder codec eol-style
 -- Scheme Procedure: make-transcoder codec eol-style handling-mode
     CODEC must be a codec; EOL-STYLE, if present, an eol-style symbol;
     and HANDLING-MODE, if present, an error-handling-mode symbol.

     EOL-STYLE may be omitted, in which case it defaults to the native
     end-of-line style of the underlying platform.  HANDLING-MODE may be
     omitted, in which case it defaults to â€˜replaceâ€™.  The result is a
     transcoder with the behavior specified by its arguments.

 -- Scheme procedure: native-transcoder
     Returns an implementation-dependent transcoder that represents a
     possibly locale-dependent â€œnativeâ€ transcoding.

 -- Scheme Procedure: transcoder-codec transcoder
 -- Scheme Procedure: transcoder-eol-style transcoder
 -- Scheme Procedure: transcoder-error-handling-mode transcoder
     These are accessors for transcoder objects; when applied to a
     transcoder returned by â€˜make-transcoderâ€™, they return the CODEC,
     EOL-STYLE, and HANDLING-MODE arguments, respectively.

 -- Scheme Procedure: bytevector->string bytevector transcoder
     Returns the string that results from transcoding the BYTEVECTOR
     according to the input direction of the transcoder.

 -- Scheme Procedure: string->bytevector string transcoder
     Returns the bytevector that results from transcoding the STRING
     according to the output direction of the transcoder.

7.6.2.16 rnrs io ports
......................

Guileâ€™s binary and textual port interface was heavily inspired by R6RS,
so many R6RS port interfaces are documented elsewhere.  Note that R6RS
ports are not disjoint from Guileâ€™s native ports, so Guile-specific
procedures will work on ports created using the R6RS API, and vice
versa.  Also note that in Guile, all ports are both textual and binary.
*Note Input and Output::, for more on Guileâ€™s core port API. The R6RS
ports module wraps Guileâ€™s I/O routines in a helper that will translate
native Guile exceptions to R6RS conditions; *Note R6RS I/O Conditions::,
for more.  *Note R6RS File Ports::, for documentation on the R6RS file
port interface.

   _Note_: The implementation of this R6RS API is not complete yet.

 -- Scheme Procedure: eof-object? obj
     *Note Binary I/O::, for documentation.

     Return a transcoder associated with the encoding of PORT.  *Note
     Encoding::, and *Note R6RS Transcoders::.

 -- Scheme Procedure: binary-port? port
     Return â€˜#tâ€™ if PORT appears to be a binary port, else return â€˜#fâ€™.
     Note that Guile does not currently distinguish between binary and
     textual ports, so this predicate is not a reliable indicator of
     whether the port was created as a binary port.  Currently, it
     returns â€˜#tâ€™ if and only if the port encoding is â€œISO-8859-1â€,
     because Guile uses this encoding when creating a binary port.
     *Note Encoding::, for more details.

 -- Scheme Procedure: textual-port? port
     Return â€˜#tâ€™ if PORT appears to be a textual port, else return â€˜#fâ€™.
     Note that Guile does not currently distinguish between binary and
     textual ports, so this predicate is not a reliable indicator of
     whether the port was created as a textual port.  Currently, it
     always returns â€˜#tâ€™, because all ports can be used for textual I/O
     in Guile.  *Note Encoding::, for more details.

 -- Scheme Procedure: transcoded-port binary-port transcoder
     The â€˜transcoded-portâ€™ procedure returns a new textual port with the
     specified TRANSCODER.  Otherwise the new textual portâ€™s state is
     largely the same as that of BINARY-PORT.  If BINARY-PORT is an
     input port, the new textual port will be an input port and will
     transcode the bytes that have not yet been read from BINARY-PORT.
     If BINARY-PORT is an output port, the new textual port will be an
     output port and will transcode output characters into bytes that
     are written to the byte sink represented by BINARY-PORT.

     As a side effect, however, â€˜transcoded-portâ€™ closes BINARY-PORT in
     a special way that allows the new textual port to continue to use
     the byte source or sink represented by BINARY-PORT, even though
     BINARY-PORT itself is closed and cannot be used by the input and

 -- Scheme Procedure: get-datum textual-input-port count
     Reads an external representation from TEXTUAL-INPUT-PORT and

     the next datum that can be parsed from the given
     TEXTUAL-INPUT-PORT, updating TEXTUAL-INPUT-PORT to point exactly

     â€˜&i/o-readâ€™ is raised.

 -- Scheme Procedure: put-datum textual-output-port datum

     external representation of DATUM to TEXTUAL-OUTPUT-PORT.  The
     specific external representation is implementation-dependent.
     However, whenever possible, an implementation should produce a
     representation for which â€˜get-datumâ€™, when reading the
     representation, will return an object equal (in the sense of

7.6.2.17 R6RS File Ports
........................

The facilities described in this section are exported by the â€˜(rnrs io
ports)â€™ module.

 -- Scheme Syntax: buffer-mode BUFFER-MODE-SYMBOL
     BUFFER-MODE-SYMBOL must be a symbol whose name is one of â€˜noneâ€™,
     â€˜lineâ€™, and â€˜blockâ€™.  The result is the corresponding symbol, and
     specifies the associated buffer mode.  *Note Buffering::, for a
     discussion of these different buffer modes.  To control the amount
     of buffering, use â€˜setvbufâ€™ instead.  Note that only the name of
     BUFFER-MODE-SYMBOL is significant.

     *Note Buffering::, for a discussion of port buffering.

 -- Scheme Procedure: buffer-mode? obj
     Returns â€˜#tâ€™ if the argument is a valid buffer-mode symbol, and
     returns â€˜#fâ€™ otherwise.

   When opening a file, the various procedures accept a â€˜file-optionsâ€™
object that encapsulates flags to specify how the file is to be opened.
A â€˜file-optionsâ€™ object is an enum-set (*note rnrs enums::) over the
symbols constituting valid file options.

   A FILE-OPTIONS parameter name means that the corresponding argument
must be a file-options object.

 -- Scheme Syntax: file-options FILE-OPTIONS-SYMBOL ...

     Each FILE-OPTIONS-SYMBOL must be a symbol.

     The â€˜file-optionsâ€™ syntax returns a file-options object that
     encapsulates the specified options.

     When supplied to an operation that opens a file for output, the
     file-options object returned by â€˜(file-options)â€™ specifies that the
     file is created if it does not exist and an exception with
     condition type â€˜&i/o-file-already-existsâ€™ is raised if it does
     exist.  The following standard options can be included to modify
     the default behavior.

     â€˜no-createâ€™
          If the file does not already exist, it is not created;
          instead, an exception with condition type
          â€˜&i/o-file-does-not-existâ€™ is raised.  If the file already
          exists, the exception with condition type
          â€˜&i/o-file-already-existsâ€™ is not raised and the file is
          truncated to zero length.
     â€˜no-failâ€™
          If the file already exists, the exception with condition type
          â€˜&i/o-file-already-existsâ€™ is not raised, even if â€˜no-createâ€™
          is not included, and the file is truncated to zero length.
     â€˜no-truncateâ€™
          If the file already exists and the exception with condition
          type â€˜&i/o-file-already-existsâ€™ has been inhibited by
          inclusion of â€˜no-createâ€™ or â€˜no-failâ€™, the file is not
          truncated, but the portâ€™s current position is still set to the
          beginning of the file.

     These options have no effect when a file is opened only for input.
     Symbols other than those listed above may be used as
     FILE-OPTIONS-SYMBOLs; they have implementation-specific meaning, if
     any.

          Note: Only the name of FILE-OPTIONS-SYMBOL is significant.

     The FILE-OPTIONS argument, which may determine various aspects of

     is implementation-dependent (and possibly transcoder-dependent).

7.6.2.21 rnrs arithmetic fixnums
................................

The â€˜(rnrs arithmetic fixnums (6))â€™ library provides procedures for
performing arithmetic operations on an implementation-dependent range of
exact integer values, which R6RS refers to as â€œfixnumsâ€.  In Guile, the
size of a fixnum is determined by the size of the â€˜SCMâ€™ type; a single
SCM struct is guaranteed to be able to hold an entire fixnum, making
fixnum computations particularly efficientâ€”(*note The SCM Type::).  On
32-bit systems, the most negative and most positive fixnum values are,
respectively, -536870912 and 536870911.

   Unless otherwise specified, all of the procedures below take fixnums
as arguments, and will raise an â€˜&assertionâ€™ condition if passed a
non-fixnum argument or an â€˜&implementation-restrictionâ€™ condition if
their result is not itself a fixnum.

The â€˜(rnrs enums (6))â€™ library provides structures and procedures for

performing set operations on lists; Guileâ€™s â€˜(rnrs enums)â€™
implementation makes use of several of them.  *Note SRFI-1 Set

     enum-set with the same universe that represents a subset containing

 -- Scheme Procedure: enum-set-member? symbol enum-set

     SYMBOL is a member of the subset specified by ENUM-SET.

     and only if ENUM-SET1 is a subset, as per â€˜enum-set-subset?â€™ of

     These procedures return, respectively, the union, intersection, and

 -- Scheme Procedure: enum-set-projection enum-set1 enum-set2
     Returns the projection of the enum-set ENUM-SET1 onto the universe

 -- Scheme Syntax: define-enumeration type-name (symbol ...)
          constructor-syntax
     Evaluates to two new definitions: A constructor bound to

     ENVIRONMENT.  This procedure is identical to the one provided by
     Guileâ€™s code library; *Note Fly Evaluation::, for documentation.

 -- Scheme Procedure: environment import-spec ...
     Constructs and returns a new environment based on the specified
     IMPORT-SPECs, which must be datum representations of the import
     specifications used with the â€˜importâ€™ form.  *Note R6RS
     Libraries::, for documentation.

7.6.2.29 rnrs mutable-pairs
...........................

The â€˜(rnrs mutable-pairs (6))â€™ library provides the â€˜set-car!â€™ and
â€˜set-cdr!â€™ procedures, which allow the â€˜carâ€™ and â€˜cdrâ€™ fields of a pair
to be modified.

   These procedures are identical to the ones provide by Guileâ€™s core
library.  *Note Pairs::, for documentation.  All pairs in Guile are
mutable; consequently, these procedures will never throw the
â€˜&assertionâ€™ condition described in the R6RS libraries specification.

7.7 R7RS Support
================

The R7RS (https://small.r7rs.org/) standard is essentially R5RS
(directly supported by Guile), plus a module facility, plus an
organization of bindings into a standard set of modules.

   Happily, the syntax for R7RS modules was chosen to be compatible with
R6RS, and so Guileâ€™s documentation there applies.  *Note R6RS
Libraries::, for more information on how to define R6RS libraries, and
their integration with Guile modules.  *Note Library Usage::, also.

7.7.1 Incompatibilities with the R7RS
-------------------------------------

As the R7RS is a much less ambitious standard than the R6RS (*note Guile
and Scheme::), it is very easy for Guile to support.  As such, Guile is
a fully conforming implementation of R7RS, with the exception of the
occasional bug and a couple of unimplemented features:

   â€¢ The R7RS specifies a syntax for reading circular data structures
     using â€œdatum labelsâ€, such as â€˜#0=(1 2 3 . #0#)â€™.  Guileâ€™s reader
     does not support this syntax currently;
     <https://bugs.gnu.org/38236>.

   â€¢ As with R6RS, a number of lexical features of R7RS conflict with
     Guileâ€™s historical syntax.  In addition to â€˜r6rs-hex-escapesâ€™ and
     â€˜hungry-eol-escapesâ€™ (*note R6RS Incompatibilities::), the
     â€˜r7rs-symbolsâ€™ reader feature needs to be explicitly enabled.

   Guile exposes a procedure in the root module to choose R7RS defaults
over Guileâ€™s historical defaults.

 -- Scheme Procedure: install-r7rs!
     Alter Guileâ€™s default settings to better conform to the R7RS.

     While Guileâ€™s defaults may evolve over time, the current changes
     that this procedure imposes are to add â€˜.slsâ€™ and â€˜.guile.slsâ€™ to
     the set of supported â€˜%load-extensionsâ€™, to better support R7RS
     conventions.  *Note Load Paths::.  â€˜install-r7rs!â€™ will also enable
     the reader options mentioned above.

   Finally, note that the â€˜--r7rsâ€™ command-line argument will call
â€˜install-r7rs!â€™ before calling user code.  R7RS users probably want to
pass this argument to their Guile.

7.7.2 R7RS Standard Libraries
-----------------------------

The R7RS organizes the definitions from R5RS into modules, and also adds
a few new definitions.

   We do not attempt to document these libraries fully here, as unlike
R6RS, there are few new definitions in R7RS relative to R5RS. Most of
their functionality is already in Guileâ€™s standard environment.  Again,
the expectation is that most Guile users will use the well-known and
well-documented Guile modules; these R7RS libraries are mostly useful to
users who want to port their code to other R7RS systems.

   As a brief overview, we note that the libraries defined by the R7RS
are as follows:

â€˜(scheme base)â€™
     The core functions, mostly corresponding to R5RS minus the elements
     listed separately below, but plus SRFI-34 error handling (*note
     SRFI-34::), bytevectors and bytevector ports (*note Bytevectors::),
     and some miscellaneous other new procedures.
â€˜(scheme case-lambda)â€™
     â€˜case-lambdaâ€™.
â€˜(scheme char)â€™
     Converting strings and characters to upper or lower case,
     predicates for if a characer is numeric, and so on.
â€˜(scheme complex)â€™
     Constructors and accessors for complex numbers.
â€˜(scheme cxr)â€™
     â€˜cddrâ€™, â€˜cadadrâ€™, and all that.
â€˜(scheme eval)â€™
     â€˜evalâ€™, but also an â€˜environmentâ€™ routine allowing a user to
     specify an environment using a module import set.
â€˜(scheme file)â€™
     â€˜call-with-input-fileâ€™ and so on.
â€˜(scheme inexact)â€™
     Routines that operate on inexact numbers: â€˜sinâ€™, â€˜finite?â€™, and so
     on.
â€˜(scheme lazy)â€™
     Promises.
â€˜(scheme load)â€™
     The â€˜loadâ€™ procedure.
â€˜(scheme process-context)â€™
     Environment variables.  *Note SRFI-98::.  Also, â€˜commmand-lineâ€™,
     â€˜emergency-exitâ€™ (like Guileâ€™s â€˜primitive-_exitâ€™), and â€˜exitâ€™.
â€˜(scheme r5rs)â€™
     The precise set of bindings exported by â€˜r5rsâ€™, but without
     â€˜transcript-offâ€™ / â€˜transcript-onâ€™, and also with the auxiliary
     syntax definitions like â€˜_â€™ or â€˜elseâ€™.  *Note Syntax Rules::, for
     more on auxiliary syntax.
â€˜(scheme read)â€™
     The â€˜readâ€™ procedure.
â€˜(scheme repl)â€™
     The â€˜interaction-environmentâ€™ procedure.
â€˜(scheme time)â€™
     â€˜current-secondâ€™, as well as â€˜current-jiffyâ€™ and
     â€˜jiffies-per-secondâ€™.  Guile uses the term â€œinternal time unitâ€ for
     what R7RS calls â€œjiffiesâ€.
â€˜(scheme write)â€™
     â€˜displayâ€™, â€˜writeâ€™, as well as â€˜write-sharedâ€™ and â€˜write-simpleâ€™.

   For complete documentation, we advise the interested user to consult
the R7RS directly (*note (r7rs)R7RS::).

7.8 Pattern Matching
====================

The â€˜(ice-9 match)â€™ module provides a â€œpattern matcherâ€, written by Alex
Shinn, and compatible with Andrew K. Wrightâ€™s pattern matcher found in
many Scheme implementations.

   A pattern matcher can match an object against several patterns and
extract the elements that make it up.  Patterns can represent any Scheme
object: lists, strings, symbols, records, etc.  They can optionally
contain â€œpattern variablesâ€.  When a matching pattern is found, an
expression associated with the pattern is evaluated, optionally with all
pattern variables bound to the corresponding elements of the object:

     (let ((l '(hello (world))))
       (match l           ;; <- the input object
         (('hello (who))  ;; <- the pattern
          who)))          ;; <- the expression evaluated upon matching
     â‡’ world

   In this example, list L matches the pattern â€˜('hello (who))â€™, because
it is a two-element list whose first element is the symbol â€˜helloâ€™ and
whose second element is a one-element list.  Here WHO is a pattern
variable.  â€˜matchâ€™, the pattern matcher, locally binds WHO to the value
contained in this one-element listâ€”i.e., the symbol â€˜worldâ€™.  An error
would be raised if L did not match the pattern.

   The same object can be matched against a simpler pattern:

     (let ((l '(hello (world))))
       (match l
         ((x y)
          (values x y))))
     â‡’ hello
     â‡’ (world)

   Here pattern â€˜(x y)â€™ matches any two-element list, regardless of the
types of these elements.  Pattern variables X and Y are bound to,
respectively, the first and second element of L.

   Patterns can be composed, and nested.  For instance, â€˜...â€™ (ellipsis)
means that the previous pattern may be matched zero or more times in a
list:

     (match lst
       (((heads tails ...) ...)
        heads))

This expression returns the first element of each list within LST.  For
proper lists of proper lists, it is equivalent to â€˜(map car lst)â€™.
However, it performs additional checks to make sure that LST and the
lists therein are proper lists, as prescribed by the pattern, raising an
error if they are not.

   Compared to hand-written code, pattern matching noticeably improves
clarity and concisenessâ€”no need to resort to series of â€˜carâ€™ and â€˜cdrâ€™
calls when matching lists, for instance.  It also improves robustness,
by making sure the input _completely_ matches the patternâ€”conversely,
hand-written code often trades robustness for conciseness.  And of
course, â€˜matchâ€™ is a macro, and the code it expands to is just as
efficient as equivalent hand-written code.

   The pattern matcher is defined as follows:

 -- Scheme Syntax: match exp clause1 clause2 ...
     Match object EXP against the patterns in CLAUSE1 CLAUSE2 ... in the
     order in which they appear.  Return the value produced by the first
     matching clause.  If no clause matches, throw an exception with key
     â€˜match-errorâ€™.

     Each clause has the form â€˜(pattern body1 body2 ...)â€™.  Each PATTERN
     must follow the syntax described below.  Each body is an arbitrary
     Scheme expression, possibly referring to pattern variables of
     PATTERN.

   The syntax and interpretation of patterns is as follows:

        patterns:                       matches:

pat ::= identifier                      anything, and binds identifier
      | _                               anything
      | ()                              the empty list
      | #t                              #t
      | #f                              #f
      | string                          a string
      | number                          a number
      | character                       a character
      | 'sexp                           an s-expression
      | 'symbol                         a symbol (special case of s-expr)
      | (pat_1 ... pat_n)               list of n elements
      | (pat_1 ... pat_n . pat_{n+1})   list of n or more
      | (pat_1 ... pat_n pat_n+1 ooo)   list of n or more, each element
                                          of remainder must match pat_n+1
      | #(pat_1 ... pat_n)              vector of n elements
      | #(pat_1 ... pat_n pat_n+1 ooo)  vector of n or more, each element
                                          of remainder must match pat_n+1
      | #&pat                           box
      | ($ record-name pat_1 ... pat_n) a record
      | (= field pat)                   a ``field'' of an object
      | (and pat_1 ... pat_n)           if all of pat_1 thru pat_n match
      | (or pat_1 ... pat_n)            if any of pat_1 thru pat_n match
      | (not pat_1 ... pat_n)           if all pat_1 thru pat_n don't match
      | (? predicate pat_1 ... pat_n)   if predicate true and all of
                                          pat_1 thru pat_n match
      | (set! identifier)               anything, and binds setter
      | (get! identifier)               anything, and binds getter
      | `qp                             a quasi-pattern
      | (identifier *** pat)            matches pat in a tree and binds
                                        identifier to the path leading
                                        to the object that matches pat

ooo ::= ...                             zero or more
      | ___                             zero or more
      | ..1                             1 or more

        quasi-patterns:                 matches:

qp  ::= ()                              the empty list
      | #t                              #t
      | #f                              #f
      | string                          a string
      | number                          a number
      | character                       a character
      | identifier                      a symbol
      | (qp_1 ... qp_n)                 list of n elements
      | (qp_1 ... qp_n . qp_{n+1})      list of n or more
      | (qp_1 ... qp_n qp_n+1 ooo)      list of n or more, each element
                                          of remainder must match qp_n+1
      | #(qp_1 ... qp_n)                vector of n elements
      | #(qp_1 ... qp_n qp_n+1 ooo)     vector of n or more, each element
                                          of remainder must match qp_n+1
      | #&qp                            box
      | ,pat                            a pattern
      | ,@pat                           a pattern

   The names â€˜quoteâ€™, â€˜quasiquoteâ€™, â€˜unquoteâ€™, â€˜unquote-splicingâ€™, â€˜?â€™,
â€˜_â€™, â€˜$â€™, â€˜andâ€™, â€˜orâ€™, â€˜notâ€™, â€˜set!â€™, â€˜get!â€™, â€˜...â€™, and â€˜___â€™ cannot be
used as pattern variables.

   Here is a more complex example:

     (use-modules (srfi srfi-9))

     (let ()
       (define-record-type person
         (make-person name friends)
         person?
         (name    person-name)
         (friends person-friends))

       (letrec ((alice (make-person "Alice" (delay (list bob))))
                (bob   (make-person "Bob" (delay (list alice)))))
         (match alice
           (($ person name (= force (($ person "Bob"))))
            (list 'friend-of-bob name))
           (_ #f))))

     â‡’ (friend-of-bob "Alice")

Here the â€˜$â€™ pattern is used to match a SRFI-9 record of type PERSON
containing two or more slots.  The value of the first slot is bound to
NAME.  The â€˜=â€™ pattern is used to apply â€˜forceâ€™ on the second slot, and
then checking that the result matches the given pattern.  In other
words, the complete pattern matches any PERSON whose second slot is a
promise that evaluates to a one-element list containing a PERSON whose
first slot is â€˜"Bob"â€™.

   The â€˜(ice-9 match)â€™ module also provides the following convenient
syntactic sugar macros wrapping around â€˜matchâ€™.

 -- Scheme Syntax: match-lambda clause1 clause2 ...
     Create a procedure of one argument that matches its argument
     against each clause, and returns the result of evaluating the
     corresponding expressions.

          (match-lambda clause1 clause2 ...)
          â‰¡
          (lambda (arg) (match arg clause1 clause2 ...))

     ((match-lambda
        (('hello (who))
         who))
      '(hello (world)))
     â‡’ world

 -- Scheme Syntax: match-lambda* clause1 clause2 ...
     Create a procedure of any number of arguments that matches its
     argument list against each clause, and returns the result of
     evaluating the corresponding expressions.

          (match-lambda* clause1 clause2 ...)
          â‰¡
          (lambda args (match args clause1 clause2 ...))

     ((match-lambda*
        (('hello (who))
         who))
      'hello '(world))
     â‡’ world

 -- Scheme Syntax: match-let ((pattern expression) ...) body
     Match each pattern to the corresponding expression, and evaluate
     the body with all matched variables in scope.  Raise an error if
     any of the expressions fail to match.  â€˜match-letâ€™ is analogous to
     named let and can also be used for recursive functions which match
     on their arguments as in â€˜match-lambda*â€™.

          (match-let (((x y) (list 1 2))
                      ((a b) (list 3 4)))
            (list a b x y))
          â‡’
          (3 4 1 2)

 -- Scheme Syntax: match-let variable ((pattern init) ...) body
     Similar to â€˜match-letâ€™, but analogously to â€œnamed letâ€, locally
     bind VARIABLE to a new procedure which accepts as many arguments as
     there are INIT expressions.  The procedure is initially applied to
     the results of evaluating the INIT expressions.  When called, the
     procedure matches each argument against the corresponding PATTERN,
     and returns the result(s) of evaluating the BODY expressions.
     *Note Iteration: while do, for more on â€œnamed letâ€.

 -- Scheme Syntax: match-let* ((variable expression) ...) body
     Similar to â€˜match-letâ€™, but analogously to â€˜let*â€™, match and bind
     the variables in sequence, with preceding match variables in scope.

          (match-let* (((x y) (list 1 2))
                       ((a b) (list x 4)))
            (list a b x y))
          â‰¡
          (match-let (((x y) (list 1 2)))
            (match-let (((a b) (list x 4)))
              (list a b x y)))
          â‡’
          (1 4 1 2)

 -- Scheme Syntax: match-letrec ((variable expression) ...) body
     Similar to â€˜match-letâ€™, but analogously to â€˜letrecâ€™, match and bind
     the variables with all match variables in scope.

   Guile also comes with a pattern matcher specifically tailored to SXML
trees, *Note sxml-match::.

7.9 Readline Support
====================

Guile comes with an interface module to the readline library (*note
(readline)Top::).  This makes interactive use much more convenient,
because of the command-line editing features of readline.  Using â€˜(ice-9
readline)â€™, you can navigate through the current input line with the
cursor keys, retrieve older command lines from the input history and
even search through the history entries.

7.9.1 Loading Readline Support
------------------------------

The module is not loaded by default and so has to be loaded and
activated explicitly.  This is done with two simple lines of code:

     (use-modules (ice-9 readline))
     (activate-readline)

   The first line will load the necessary code, and the second will
activate readlineâ€™s features for the REPL. If you plan to use this
module often, you should save these to lines to your â€˜.guileâ€™ personal
startup file.

   You will notice that the REPLâ€™s behavior changes a bit when you have
loaded the readline module.  For example, when you press Enter before
typing in the closing parentheses of a list, you will see the
â€œcontinuationâ€ prompt, three dots: â€˜...â€™ This gives you a nice visual
feedback when trying to match parentheses.  To make this even easier,
â€œbouncing parenthesesâ€ are implemented.  That means that when you type
in a closing parentheses, the cursor will jump to the corresponding
opening parenthesis for a short time, making it trivial to make them
match.

   Once the readline module is activated, all lines entered
interactively will be stored in a history and can be recalled later
using the cursor-up and -down keys.  Readline also understands the Emacs
keys for navigating through the command line and history.

   When you quit your Guile session by evaluating â€˜(quit)â€™ or pressing
Ctrl-D, the history will be saved to the file â€˜.guile_historyâ€™ and read
in when you start Guile for the next time.  Thus you can start a new
Guile session and still have the (probably long-winded) definition
expressions available.

   You can specify a different history file by setting the environment
variable â€˜GUILE_HISTORYâ€™.  And you can make Guile specific
customizations to your â€˜.inputrcâ€™ by testing for application â€˜Guileâ€™
(*note (readline)Conditional Init Constructs::).  For instance to define
a key inserting a matched pair of parentheses,

     $if Guile
       "\C-o": "()\C-b"
     $endif

7.9.2 Readline Options
----------------------

The readline interface module can be tweaked in a few ways to better
suit the userâ€™s needs.  Configuration is done via the readline moduleâ€™s
options interface, in a similar way to the evaluator and debugging
options (*note Runtime Options::).

 -- Scheme Procedure: readline-options
 -- Scheme Procedure: readline-enable option-name
 -- Scheme Procedure: readline-disable option-name
 -- Scheme Syntax: readline-set! option-name value
     Accessors for the readline options.  Note that unlike the
     enable/disable procedures, â€˜readline-set!â€™ is syntax, which expects
     an unquoted option name.

   Here is the list of readline options generated by typing
â€˜(readline-options 'help)â€™ in Guile.  You can also see the default
values.

     history-file    yes     Use history file.
     history-length  200     History length.
     bounce-parens   500     Time (ms) to show matching opening parenthesis
                             (0 = off).
     bracketed-paste yes     Disable interpretation of control characters
                             in pastes.

   The readline options interface can only be used _after_ loading the
readline module, because it is defined in that module.

7.9.3 Readline Functions
------------------------

The following functions are provided by

     (use-modules (ice-9 readline))

   There are two ways to use readline from Scheme code, either make
calls to â€˜readlineâ€™ directly to get line by line input, or use the
readline port below with all the usual reading functions.

 -- Function: readline [prompt]
     Read a line of input from the user and return it as a string
     (without a newline at the end).  PROMPT is the prompt to show, or
     the default is the string set in â€˜set-readline-prompt!â€™ below.

          (readline "Type something: ") â‡’ "hello"

 -- Function: set-readline-input-port! port
 -- Function: set-readline-output-port! port
     Set the input and output port the readline function should read
     from and write to.  PORT must be a file port (*note File Ports::),
     and should usually be a terminal.

     The default is the â€˜current-input-portâ€™ and â€˜current-output-portâ€™
     (*note Default Ports::) when â€˜(ice-9 readline)â€™ loads, which in an
     interactive user session means the Unix â€œstandard inputâ€ and
     â€œstandard outputâ€.

7.9.3.1 Readline Port
.....................

 -- Function: readline-port
     Return a buffered input port (*note Buffered Input::) which calls
     the â€˜readlineâ€™ function above to get input.  This port can be used
     with all the usual reading functions (â€˜readâ€™, â€˜read-charâ€™, etc),
     and the user gets the interactive editing features of readline.

     Thereâ€™s only a single readline port created.  â€˜readline-portâ€™
     creates it when first called, and on subsequent calls just returns
     what it previously made.

 -- Function: activate-readline
     If the â€˜current-input-portâ€™ is a terminal (*note â€˜isatty?â€™:
     Terminals and Ptys.) then enable readline for all reading from
     â€˜current-input-portâ€™ (*note Default Ports::) and enable readline
     features in the interactive REPL (*note The REPL::).

          (activate-readline)
          (read-char)

     â€˜activate-readlineâ€™ enables readline on â€˜current-input-portâ€™ simply
     by a â€˜set-current-input-portâ€™ to the â€˜readline-portâ€™ above.  An
